p.src: Overview: The one-dimensional supersymmetry algebra of the preceding lecture involved only the Hamiltonian. Lorentz invariance now forces energy to rejoin the spatial momentum, and the supercharges must become two-component spinors. We reach that algebra by returning first to a massless Weyl fermion and its Hamiltonian $H=\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf p$. We then represent the supercharges as differential operators on four-dimensional superspace, isolate chiral superfields with the constraint $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\Phi=0$, and use superspace integration to construct a concrete field theory. The successive choices $\Phi^\dagger\Phi$, $\Phi^2$, and $\Phi^3$ produce propagation, equal boson–fermion masses, Yukawa interactions, and a related scalar interaction. The auxiliary field $F$ makes these relations transparent, while the closing loop diagrams show why supersymmetry softens ultraviolet sensitivity.

p.src: Begin with the physical distinction between massive and massless particles. Take a massive spin-$\tfrac12$ particle moving in the direction of its spin. A Lorentz-invariant massive theory must consequently contain both helicities.

p.src:
The odd coordinates must now transform like Weyl spinors: $\theta^\alpha=(\theta^1,\theta^2),
\qquad
\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}=(\bar\theta^{\dot1},\bar\theta^{\dot2}).$ The bar denotes complex conjugation, and the dot distinguishes the conjugate Lorentz representation. There are two complex, or four real, Grassmann components. A general even superfield $\mathcal S=\mathcal S(x^\mu,\theta^\alpha,\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha})$ therefore has a finite Grassmann expansion. Its highest monomial is $\theta^2\bar\theta^2
\equiv
(\theta^1\theta^2)(\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}),$ the product of all four independent odd coordinates. The coefficient of this monomial is commonly called the $D$-component.

The supercharges also carry spinor indices. In four-dimensional $N=1$ supersymmetry their algebra is $\begin{aligned}\{Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}
&=2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu,
\\
\{Q_\alpha,Q_\beta\}&=0,
&
\{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha},\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}&=0,
\\
[P_\mu,Q_\alpha]&=0,
&
[P_\mu,\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}]&=0,
&
[P_\mu,P_\nu]&=0.
\end{aligned}$ The factor of two is conventional. The matrix $\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}$ contracts the vector index on $P_\mu$ and leaves precisely the two spinor indices appearing on the left.

p.src:
Propagation came from a $D$-term. Mass comes from the chiral integral. Choose the conventional normalization $W_2(\Phi)=\frac12m\Phi^2.$ The $\theta^2$ component is $\left.W_2(\Phi)\right|_{\theta^2}
=m\phi F-\frac12m\psi\psi.$ Together with the conjugate term, the component Lagrangian becomes $\begin{aligned}\mathcal L
={}&
\partial_\mu\phi^\ast\partial^\mu\phi
+i\bar\psi\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi
+F^\ast F
\notag\\
&+m\phi F+m^\ast\phi^\ast F^\ast
-\frac12m\psi\psi
-\frac12m^\ast\bar\psi\bar\psi.
\end{aligned}$ The fermion bilinear is a Majorana mass for the Weyl field. The $F$-equations are algebraic: $F^\ast=-m\phi,
\qquad
F=-m^\ast\phi^\ast.$ Substitution gives $\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{on\ shell}}={}&
\partial_\mu\phi^\ast\partial^\mu\phi
+i\bar\psi\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi\\
&-|m|^2|\phi|^2\\
&-\frac12\left(m\psi\psi+m^\ast\bar\psi\bar\psi\right).
\end{aligned}$ Thus the scalar mass and fermion mass are both $|m|$. In the board’s diagrammatic language, a scalar turns locally into $F$ through one $m\phi F$ insertion and immediately turns back through its conjugate. Two insertions supply $|m|^2|\phi|^2$, exactly the scalar mass term found by solving Eq. [eq:l8-mass-F-equations].

p.src: At one loop the leading ultraviolet-sensitive pieces cancel between the complete bosonic and fermionic contributions. ja: 1ループでは、主要な紫外に敏感な部分が、完全なボソン的寄与とフェルミオン的寄与の間で相殺する。同じ対称性が、Ward恒等式と非繰り込み性によって高次を組織する。この主張は対称性に関連した和についてのものであり、すべてのグラフが文字通り1対1で相殺するということではない。波動関数の繰り込み、有限の効果、その他の対称性を保つ補正は残りうる。これが超空間で理論を構築する実際的な力である。すなわち、質量の等しさと結合定数の間の関係が、個々のファインマン積分を評価する前に強制される。 (編集上の補足: 黒板は相殺をより広く述べている。本文は標準的な限定を与えている。)

p.src: Exact supersymmetry is not visible in the observed particle spectrum, so the next problem is how the symmetry can be broken while retaining enough of its ultraviolet control to be useful. Those are the questions to which the remaining lectures turn.
